Schwa [ə] plus alveolar trill or tap [ɾ], from the root mar- 'to die'
Reduced vowel [ə], a linking syllable in the Avestan form
Long [aː] plus alveolar stop [t], the abstract noun ending '-ness, -ity'

pronunciation.approximation: ah-muh-ruh-TAHT — the middle syllables are light and quick, while the final 'tah' is long and emphatic.

pronunciation.note: Amərətāt is Tier-1: the macron on the long final ā is a distinctive feature the ASCII form loses. As one of the Amesha Spentas, her name is an abstract noun meaning 'immortality' personified.

domains.title: Immortality in Bloom
domains.subtitle: Plants, Longevity, and the Amesha Spenta
domains.lead: Amərətāt is the Amesha Spenta of immortality and plants in Zoroastrianism. She embodies the divine promise that the soul endures and that the earth's vegetation sustains life. Where her sister Haurvatāt guards water and wholeness, Amərətāt guards the plant kingdom and the final victory over death. She is the green hope at the heart of Zoroastrian cosmology.

cards.name: Guardian of Plants
cards.desc: Every tree, herb, and grain falls under her protection as the divine patron of vegetation — the fourth of the seven creations.

cards.name: Immortality
cards.desc: Her name means 'non-death'; she is the spiritual force that promises life beyond death, sealed by the white haoma.

cards.name: Pair with Haurvatāt
cards.desc: She and Haurvatāt (wholeness/health) are invoked together in every Yasna as the complementary gifts of body and eternity.

cards.name: The Final Renovation
cards.desc: At Frashokereti, Amərətāt's domain will flourish in a world without death or decay.

mythology.lead: Amərətāt does not have a long narrative mythology of her own; her stories are the cosmogony's fourth chapter, the Yasna's nightly rite, and the eschatology's final meal. As one of the seven Holy Immortals she helps govern the created world — and the war over her domain, the green one, is the war we call agriculture.

myths.title: The Creation of Plants
myths.text: Zoroastrian cosmogony counts seven good creations, and the fourth is the green one: plants, urwarō, fashioned by Ahura Mazdā as the roof of the food chain — beneath sky, water, and earth, above cattle and man (Bundaahišn 1, 3). To this creation he appoints Amərətāt, 'non-death-ness', her name locking the root mar-, 'to die', behind a private prefix. Ahriman's reply is the counter-creation of decay — drought, frost, locust, and blight — so that the struggle between growth and rot becomes a cosmic front on which every farmer is a soldier. The pairing is exact and the lesson practical. The calendar keeps the assignment: the fifth day of every month and the month of Amurdād still bear her name. To plant, water, and weed is to fight on the right side of a cosmic war — gardening is the original act of religion.

myths.title: The Bodies of the Righteous
myths.text: At Frashogard the resurrection bodies will need more than spirit — they will need the food of immortality, and the texts supply it: the white haoma, the paradisal plant of the renovation, offered to the risen so that they shall not die again (Bundaahišn 30; Zātspram 35). Amərətāt's gift is realized through her sister-domains: the pressed plant of Haoma's rite, the pure water of Haurvatāt's, the consecrated fire of Ašavahišta's — the whole ecology of the seven creations serving one meal. Immortality in this scheme is not an escape from matter but matter's perfection: the same bodies, finally unwound from decay. The image stayed with the tradition's artists, who fill manuscript margins with paradisal gardens for precisely this scene. The resurrection meal is a garden and a spring — eternal life arrives as ecology restored.

myths.title: Haoma and the Yasna
myths.text: The nightly Yasna enacts her domain: the priest pounds haoma twigs in water, strains the draught, offers it with milk and the word — the triad of plant, water, and prayer that recreates the original goodness of the seven creations in microcosm (Yasna 9–11). The litany of Yasna 1 invokes 'Haurvatāt and Amərətāt' beside the other Immortals, keeping the two sisters together as the tradition always does; the congregation's sip binds each worshipper to the plant-world she guards. Parsi and Irani priests perform some form of this rite daily. The offering is never wasted: the pressed remains are returned to the earth, completing the circuit the myth describes. Every draught passes through her domain on its way to the cup. Her sacrament is agriculture sanctified: the oldest living ritual on earth is, among other things, her liturgy.

myths.title: Taurvi and Zairi, the Twin Destroyers
myths.text: The demon lists of the younger Avesta are a dark mirror of the Immortals: against Haurvatāt and Amərətāt stand the twin she-demons Taurvi and Zairi — scorching heat and blight, in the usual gloss — sent to wither water and green life (Vendidad 10.9; Yašt 1). Where the sisters guard, gardens drink; where the demons advance, harvests fail and the wells run bitter. The pairing turns ecology into ethics: famine is not weather but warfare, and the blighted field is a battlefield report from a front that never closes. The tradition's answer is neither fatalism nor magic but husbandry — tend, water, protect. The pairing is mnemonic as much as theological: two sisters, two demons — a symmetry priests could recite and farmers could trust. Amərətāt's mythology is a reminder that 'immortality' begins in the seed catalog and the water share.

lore.syncretism: Amərətāt is one of a pair with Haurvatāt, and the two are often worshipped together as guardians of water/plants and health/immortality. Their names passed into Middle Persian as Amurdād and Hordād, and they are still commemorated in the Zoroastrian calendar. The Greek concept of ambrosia is closer than a loose parallel: Greek ambrotos, 'immortal', and ambrosia descend from the same Proto-Indo-European privative formation *n̥-mr̥-to-, 'undying', built on the root *mer-, 'to die' — the very root that, with the Iranian abstract suffix -tāt, produces Amərətāt; Sanskrit amṛta is the same formation again.
lore.culturalLegacy: Amərətāt remains a focus of Zoroastrian devotion as the divine guardian of vegetation and the promise of eternal life. Her name survives in the Zoroastrian calendar and in the prayers offered to the Amesha Spentas. In ecological readings of Zoroastrianism, Amərətāt is invoked as the sacred dimension of plant life and the religious duty to protect the earth's green cover. She is a reminder that immortality in this tradition is not escape from the world but the world's final healing.
lore.extendedMeditation: Amərətāt asks us to see a tree as more than timber and a field as more than calories. Plants are the visible form of immortality: they transform sunlight, water, and soil into life that outlasts the individual seed. In a time of deforestation and agricultural crisis, her message is urgent: to harm the plant world is to attack the very possibility of sustained life. To honor Amərətāt is to plant, to protect, and to hope that what grows today will outlive us.

lore.archaeology: Amərətāt is invoked in Avestan liturgical texts and in Sasanian-era inscriptions and seals that name the Amesha Spentas. Zoroastrian ritual vessels, fire temples, and manuscript illuminations associate her with vegetation and the paradisal garden. The haoma rite, though now performed with substitutes in many communities, preserves the plant-offering at the center of her domain.
